9be6b25946e149fbf7c8c04a904092e8925e12d0f501bb1b4257b013464122d0
Identification: SHA-256 digest record, collected as Win64.NukeSped.shasum.
Verdict: BENIGN. Exactly 65 bytes: the ASCII digest
931f062a629950ad6fb85b83262cc3f730a6e94d43a27b48f7fd857f7722c6ba
followed by LF. No executable, script, URL, dependency, or encoded payload.
The filename describes the referenced sample, not these inert bytes. Likely

b80d07610b81bddb3d7f30a207a2e134b559e06b8440598a926f3a9c1d439218
Identification: ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe 25.2.4.9229, 608024 bytes.
Verdict: BENIGN for this isolated product component; deployment authorization
remains unknown. Decompiled Main dispatches RunFile/RunFileElevated, StartService,
Rerun and RunRole. Ordinary startup parses a relay/session query or URL from argv
or ClickOnce ActivationUri and creates SocketEndPointManager. No fixed relay,
session token, instance key or campaign configuration is embedded in this file.
The external configuration and installed companion files were not supplied.

Traced IncomingMessage dispatch through clipboard synchronization, streamed file
copy into configured/temporary directories, and optional RunFileAsync execution.
RunFileAsync restarts the client with a RunFile or RunFileElevated argument;
WindowsExtensions.StartProcessInSameDirectory uses Process.Start and the runas
verb for requested elevation. No UAC bypass was observed. RunFileAsync also calls
TryUnblockFile on the current client executable; the release Windows dependency
implements this by deleting its :Zone.Identifier stream. This is a noteworthy
security-related product behavior, not evidence of a malicious deployment here.
StartService launches ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe, waits for its exit status,
and may use explicit credentials or runas. Its preparation sets a directory ACL
allowing Everyone ReadAndExecute, not arbitrary write access.

Screen capture uses DXGI or GDI/PrintWindow and a separate CopyFromScreen JPEG
thumbnail path; thumbnails are hashed with MD5 and returned in GuestInfo messages.
Keyboard/input control, audio, clipboard, file transfer, remote printing, host
information and consent dialogs correspond to remote support functionality.
Debugger.IsAttached opens a diagnostic TraceForm; it does not suppress execution.
Base64 decoding in ExtractManifestAttachmentsIfFirstRun recovers filename/data
pairs from an external deployment manifest's XML comments into CreateNew files.
No such external manifest or attachment payload was supplied. Framework reflection
loads named Microsoft WPF/printing assemblies. No custom obfuscated payload,
packed stage, credential-store harvesting, security-product interference or
injected executable was found in these bytes. Compiler-generated anonymous
classes and modern Roslyn switch lowering are not malware obfuscation. An ILSpy
9 switch-transform failure was bypassed by disabling SwitchStatementOnString;
relevant C# and IL paths were then recovered.

13f8cfe4648b807a0cbddd653c75254b60d1951e11e715f4e5a1a2c9ab29360b
Identification: ScreenConnect.WindowsFileManager.exe 25.2.4.9229, 81688 bytes.
Verdict: BENIGN for this isolated interactive component. Main hardens DLL loading,
enables WinForms, installs thread-specific WH_GETMESSAGE/WH_CALLWNDPROCRET and
window-event hooks, then presents IFileOpenDialog titled ScreenConnect File
Manager. The hooks reroute mouse wheel input and customize menu drawing, icons,
window layout and tree expansion. They are not a keyboard logger or remote hook.
The default folder comes from ProfilesDirectory. The dialog exposes hidden files
and does not add recent-document entries. OnFileOk launches the selected shell
item with Process.Start and UseShellExecute=true. No network connection, embedded
relay configuration, service registration, credential theft, or payload decoding
was found in this component. Remote operation would require another component.

Packaging and independent comparison (both assemblies)
Both are IL-only, strong-name-marked PE assemblies, with coherent product/version
resources and reproducible-build markers. Their future-looking COFF timestamps
are build metadata, not demonstrated timestomping. Neither has managed embedded
resources. Their certificate-table unsigned attributes contain only Microsoft's
RFC3161 timestamp token, followed by zero alignment padding, not launch settings.
Authenticode content digests match and signer cryptography verifies. Signing times
are April 8, 2025, 18:36:29 UTC (client) and 18:35:30 UTC (file manager).

The shared Connectwise, LLC certificate has SHA-256 thumbprint
82b4e7924d5bed84fb16ddf8391936eb301479cec707dc14e23bc22b8cdeae28
and serial 0B9360051BCCF66642998998D5BA97CE. osslsigncode fetched and verified
DigiCert's CRL, whose reason code is Key Compromise, with an effective date of
August 17, 2022. ConnectWise states its 2025 rotation was not caused by a
certificate compromise; it was required because prior customization data no
longer met trust standards. Current chain/revocation validation fails, so retain
a suspicious revoked-certificate observation without claiming the key was
stolen; neither sample has an observed hostile trait.
CRL: http://crl3.digicert.com/DigiCertTrustedG4CodeSigningRSA4096SHA3842021CA1.crl
The vendor describes certificate revocation and later removal of post-signing
configuration customizations; this supplies product context, not authorization:
https://www.connectwise.com/blog/new-era-remote-access-security

Fetched ScreenConnect_25.2.4.9229_Release.msi from Comodo's patch distribution:
https://cdn-patchportal-one.comodo.com/portal/packages/spm/ScreenConnect/x64/ScreenConnect_25.2.4.9229_Release.msi
MSI SHA-256: 0dabef8ee019bc34bf315794df0f5321ee8122e18d87411ab5f79f6ef73f46a0
Its MSI signature digests match; it uses the same revoked certificate. Static 7z
extraction produced byte-identical copies of BOTH submitted assemblies:
filF23135311FD413DA3A6A8DD4B38FBBC4 = client, SHA-256 b80d07610b81...
filC1D18007D3175279B0EDD654D18B0CA5 = file manager, SHA-256 13f8cfe4648b...
This independent release distribution comparison strengthens the ordinary-product
identification; it does not override revocation or prove authorized installation.
Fetched release dependencies ScreenConnect.Core, ScreenConnect.Windows and
ScreenConnect.Client were inspected with ILSpy. SocketEndPointManager constructs
relay:// from supplied Host/Port, retries connections, performs RSA secret-key
exchange and starts a secure channel. No fixed attacker endpoint was found in
that path. WindowsExtensions confirms the execution, hardening and unblocking
helpers described above. Supplied samples' dependency copies remain unknown.
Other embedded URLs are certificate authority/OCSP/CRL references, not C2.
The provided Triage pages were inaccessible; sandbox deployment context could not
be verified. PUA/RemoteAdmin/Hacktool labels are consistent with powerful remote
access software, its abuse potential, and revoked signing. No supplied evidence
establishes that these exact components were used without authorization. BENIGN
therefore means the isolated-artifact balance of evidence, not a clean deployment
attestation; the queue's sighted-quarantine handling remains appropriate.

Trait corrections and placement review
- set_Item now requires a complete word; set_ItemsEnabled, set_Items and
  set_ItemHeight no longer serve as indexer-setter evidence. Existing actual
  set_Item references remain notable. This is a matcher correction, not demotion.
- The Service.exe filename matcher moves from os/service/identity to
  fs/path/basename::service-suffix-executable-reference. Its evidence is an
  executable basename suffix, with no directory path or service-registration
  operation. It establishes no running service. Matcher and criticality are
  preserved; named script/source groups replace the former ten-type enumeration,
  intentionally covering the same neutral reference in additional source types.
- Audited source identity and service-parent selectors and target basename
  selectors. Two exact consumers now reference the moved ID. The directory
  consumer multi-db-service-kill-pe becomes stop AND (remaining identities OR
  moved suffix), preserving the original stop AND identity condition rather than
  accidentally counting the new alternative as an independent second role.
- IFileOpenDialog is a Windows shell file-picker widget interface; its new notable
  trait belongs in ui/controls/widget. It claims an API reference, not file access,
  theft or covert collection. Existing UI hook and process-launch traits remain.
- No product identity exclusion suppresses these components' capabilities or
  revoked-certificate finding. No hostile findings were added for legitimate
  remote-administration functionality.

Focused controls
IndexerPicker.dll contains a real CLR indexer setter, IFileOpenDialog interface,
and ExampleService.exe literal. ItemsEnabled.dll instead contains set_ItemsEnabled,
IFileOpenDialogEvents and ExampleService.dll; all three target observations must
be absent. These are inert compiled controls, not executed. Sources accompany the
DLLs. Build with .NET SDK 8 targeting net8.0, deterministic compilation, no packages.
Run: python3 testdata/taxonomy/screenconnect-managed-components/check.py
Analysis commands, complete facts, scans, IL and decompiler output are retained
under the task scratch/analysis directory. Each requested sample received initial
atomscan and cleave facts analysis; final atomscan runs confirm retained targets.
